title: Dynamics and restraint in Chicago playing
summary: They discuss use of soft playing, 'underwater', and whether restraint came from not knowing what notes to play.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What the word "jazz" means: origins, Dixieland and labels

blocks.x: Would you call the loudness a feature of dynamics, or just they played loud all the time?

Fortunately, they used dynamics. They played in contrast. They played many things like, well, even Napoleon and Miff were talking about it, although they weren't doing much about it before. They called it underwater. They'd go down to the punny trombone underwater, was their phrase. And they would get way down.

And frequently it would lead to a breathing kind of effect, where the soft playing would be an intake of breath, and then a little later on you'd let it all out. Yeah. Although the phrase might be pretty long, that is, dynamics might extend 16 bars, you thought of it sometimes as a breathing effect as well as underwater and out.
That's true. It was a conscious use of restraint, for the value that restraint had.

There's been some talk about restraint in the Chicago style being a result of not knowing what notes to play, and so you wait a little while until you find one. Do you think there's any truth to that?
Well, it was true in the early days of the Austin Band. There's no question about it. When they really didn't know what they were playing.

Well, I'm sure that it arose from a number of experiments, and some of these features do seem... Oh, my God. All right. Thank you, Mary. Goodbye. Goodbye. I'm sure that... You were talking about dynamics before...
